client: I just can't bring myself to go to family dinners anymore. Every time I walk into my parents' house, I keep expecting to see Grandma in her usual chair, and when she's not there it feels like someone punched me in the chest. Everyone else seems to be moving on, but I just sit there feeling this awful emptiness.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying such deep grief, and that empty chair is like a fresh wound every time you walk in. The way your voice gets so quiet when you talk about this tells me how deeply this pain sits in your heart. Would it help to explore how we might honor your grandma's memory while also gently challenging the thought that everyone else has moved on?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know if honoring her memory will help...it just makes me miss her more. Everyone else in the family seems fine now, but I still wake up expecting to hear her voice in the kitchen. 

The thought that people have moved on makes me feel even more alone with this pain. Like I'm the only one who can't let go properly.
therapist: Your voice speeds up when you talk about feeling alone in your grief - it sounds like this loneliness is adding another layer of pain on top of your loss. Let's gently examine whether "moving on" might look different for different people, rather than meaning they care any less.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess I do rush when talking about it because I'm afraid if I slow down, the loneliness will swallow me whole. But the idea that people grieve differently... that makes me angry sometimes, because it feels like an excuse when others seem to have moved on so quickly while I'm still drowning. 

I want to believe they still care, but when they stop mentioning her name or asking how I'm doing, it just confirms my worst fear - that I'm alone in remembering.
therapist: Your voice gets so small and quick when you share this - I can hear how terrifying it feels to face that loneliness. Let's unpack this together: what if people aren't mentioning her because they're afraid of upsetting you, rather than because they've forgotten?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I never thought about it that way... but honestly, even if they're trying to protect me, it just makes me feel more alone. Like she's becoming this unspoken thing that no one can acknowledge, and that hurts almost worse than if they brought her up carelessly. 

I don't know how to tell people what I need from them without feeling like I'm being needy or difficult.
therapist: Your voice gets so high and rushed when you talk about this - I can hear how much it hurts to feel like her memory is being tucked away. Let's explore how you might gently share what you need - not as being needy, but as honoring your very human need for connection in grief.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I just don't know how to bring it up without making people uncomfortable. Every time I try to talk about my mom, I see people shift in their seats or change the subject. It makes me feel like I'm being too much, like my grief is an inconvenience to them. 

The idea of sharing what I need sounds terrifying because what if they pull away even more? I already feel so alone in this.
therapist: Your voice gets so high and fast when you talk about this - I can hear how scared you are of pushing people away while also desperately needing their support. Let's try this: what if we practiced some gentle ways to share your needs that might feel less risky to you?

client: I don't know... every time I try to tell people what I need, it feels like I'm being too much. What if practicing makes me sound rehearsed or fake? I already feel like people can tell how needy I am just by looking at me.
therapist: Your voice gets so high and rushed when you talk about this - I can hear how afraid you are of being judged for your very normal human needs. Let's challenge this thought together: what if people actually want to support you but just don't know how, rather than seeing you as "too much"?

client:
I don't know... it's hard to believe people would actually want to support me. Every time I've tried opening up before, I either got brushed off or people seemed uncomfortable. Maybe they just don't want to deal with my problems. 

That thought about people not knowing how to help - it sounds nice, but it feels like wishful thinking. I notice my hands are shaking just talking about this. What if they really do think I'm too much?
therapist: Your voice gets so high and fast when you share this - I can hear how deeply these past experiences have shaken your trust in reaching out. Let's pause for a moment and breathe together, because I can see how much this hurts - both the grief itself and the fear of being a burden. client:
I guess I can try looking at examples, but honestly most people do pull away when I start opening up. Like last week when I told my friend about missing my dad, she just changed the subject to her dating life. It makes me feel like my grief is too heavy for anyone to handle. 

I don't know if it's really about their discomfort - maybe I'm just bad at sharing in a way that doesn't push people away. When you suggest breathing, I get frustrated because it feels like we're avoiding the real issue that people don't want to be there for me.
therapist: I hear how deeply painful it is when people change the subject like that - your voice gets so high and fast when you describe it, like you're reliving that hurt all over again. Let's honor both truths here: your friend's response was genuinely disappointing, and at the same time, we can explore whether this one example means everyone will pull away. Would you be willing to look at whether there might be other people in your life who could handle this better?

client:
I guess there are a couple people who might listen better, but I keep thinking about how my closest friend reacted. It makes me scared to try opening up to anyone else now. What if they all just want to change the subject when things get too heavy? 

I know you're saying not everyone will pull away, but it's hard to believe that when the person I trusted most did exactly that. It makes me feel like maybe my problems are just too much for people.

client:

But you're right, my voice does get all shaky when I talk about this. It's like my body remembers that rejection even when my mind tries to move on.
